item.title: Lead isotope evidence for Antarctic Ice Sheet changes in the Weddell Sea sector since the Last Glacial Maximum
item.dc:creator: Huang Huang, Yuanyang Hu, Marcus Gutjahr, Florian Kirsch, Lijuan Lu, Jianjun Zou, … (+4)
item.description:
Boreas — matched: ice sheet, subglacial, Antarctic, Antarctica, polar, meltwater, ocean circulation, last glacial maximum, LGM, Holocene, sediment core, sea level
The Weddell Sea influences global ocean circulation and sea level through modulating Antarctic Bottom Water formation and Antarctic Ice Sheet discharges, but the history of ice‐sheet dynamics in this region remains poorly constrained due to limited well‐dated geological records. To provide a new geochemical perspective on ice‐sheet dynamics since the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM), this study presents paired authigenic and detrital Pb isotope records from sediment core PS1599‐3 recovered from the continental slope north of the Filchner Trough. Comparison with Antarctic Pb isotope provinces indicates that both detrital and authigenic Pb signatures were possibly sourced from a Shackleton Range‐like region in the south‐eastern Weddell Sea sector of East Antarctica. This suggests that dominant upstream drainage sources remained broadly stable throughout the last ~23 ka. We interpret the downcore Pb isotope variations to primarily reflect changes in the delivery of subglacial weathering‐derived Pb associated with grounding‐line dynamics in the Filchner Trough. Authigenic 206 Pb/ 204 Pb ratios show a sharp increase at ~23 ka, followed by two decreases at ~20 and 11–9 ka. We suggest that a re‐advance of grounded ice near the LGM was followed by initial retreat at ~20 ka and further grounding‐line retreat or reorganization during the Early Holocene. These findings highlight the use of authigenic Pb isotopes as potential tracers for reconstructing polar ice‐sheet dynamics and meltwater influences.

item.title: Holocene water mass structure changes in Lake Nurume, Lützow-Holm Bay, East Antarctica
item.dc:creator: Takeshige Ishiwa, Kota Katsuki, Yuki Tokuda, Takuya Itaki, Satoshi Sasaki, Kaihe Yamazaki, … (+4)
item.category: Progress in Earth and Planetary Science
item.description:
Progress in Earth and Planetary Science — matched: ice sheet, Antarctica, Holocene, sediment core, glacial isostatic adjustment, sea level
Abstract Paleoenvironmental reconstructions using sediments from isolation basins including lakes are useful approaches to obtain evidence of sea-level and ice-sheet changes in Antarctica. However, a detailed study using multiple sediment cores of how isolation basins respond to external forcings is needed to improve the accuracy of paleoenvironmental reconstructions. We reconstructed how the water mass structure of Lake Nurume, located in Langhovde, Lützow-Holm Bay, East Antarctica, changed in response to sea-level and ice-sheet changes during the Holocene using sediments from different water depths and nearby trenches. Sedimentary observations, diatom analyses, and X-ray fluorescence core scanner analyses were conducted to reconstruct the three-dimensional characterization of water mass structure combined with the paleotopographic reconstruction using glacial isostatic adjustment modelling. Sedimentation resumed at approximately 6.6 cal kyr BP when the lake became ice-free and marine conditions, as evidenced by the presence of marine diatoms and shell fossils. At approximately 2.0 cal kyr BP, laminated structures appeared in sediment cores, accompanied by a decrease in benthic diatoms. This transition is interpreted as a response to ice-sheet readvance, whereby the ice margin approached the lake, increasing freshwater input and reducing vertical mixing. The resulting stratification caused anoxic conditions in the bottom water. Finally, at approximately 0.5 cal kyr BP, the lake became completely isolated from the sea, establishing its current water mass structure. These findings contribute to more accurate paleoenvironmental reconstructions such as sea-level and ice-sheet changes using sediments from isolation basins in Antarctica.

item.title: Atmospheric stabilization of the East Antarctic ice sheet under warming
item.dc:creator: Kyung-Sook Yun, Axel Timmermann
item.description:
Nature Climate Change — matched: ice sheet, Antarctic, Antarctica, Greenland, climate change
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02791-x The long-term response of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets to warming is often studied using ice-only simulations. Here the authors use a coupled ice–atmosphere–ocean model and find that East Antarctica remains stable even under higher warming because changes in atmospheric circulation increase precipitation sensitivity.

item.title: Workshop report: Lake KINneret Drilling (KIND) – reconstructing Pliocene–Quaternary hydroclimate and seismic history of the Levant
item.dc:creator: Adi Torfstein, Eshly Aizenshtat-Soffer, Moshe Armon, Catherine Beck, S. L. Goldstein, Hannah Hartung, … (+17)
item.description:
Scientific Drilling — matched: Pliocene, Quaternary, sediment core, climate change, global warming
The southern Levant extends between the hyperarid Sahara–Arabia Desert belt in the south and the temperate Mediterranean climate zone in the north, making the regional hydroclimate extremely sensitive to even small perturbations of global climate. The region further served as a major pathway for the “out-of-Africa” dispersal of fauna, flora, and hominins throughout the Quaternary, as well as for human cultural development from the Paleolithic to the Neolithic. Spanning the length of the Levant is the Dead Sea Transform (DST) that transfers the opening at the Red Sea in the south to the collision at the Taurus Mountains in the north. Pull-apart basins along the DST host the hypersaline Dead Sea and freshwater Lake Kinneret, whose sedimentary records document the regional hydroclimate and seismic history. Lake Kinneret (a.k.a. the Sea of Galilee) is the largest freshwater lake in the Levant, whose precursors have deposited a thick sequence of lacustrine sediments since the late Miocene. Seismic profiles across the tectonically subsiding basin in the middle of the modern lake, as well as existing short sediment cores, indicate that the sedimentary sequences are generally bounded by two N–S-striking longitudinal faults and generally maintain stratigraphic order. The sedimentary column is dominated by primary authigenic calcite, whose chemical and isotopic composition documents regional hydrology and lacustrine conditions from at least the Pliocene. Accordingly, the sedimentary record of Lake Kinneret holds the potential to serve as one of the longest and most highly resolved lacustrine records since the Pliocene, yielding sub-centennial records of hydroclimate, paleoseismicity, geomagnetism, and paleobotanics in a region of fundamental importance for the global understanding of climate change, tectonics, and human evolution. The Lake KINneret Drilling (KIND) project aims to establish an exceptionally long Pliocene–Quaternary chronostratigraphic reference record that will contribute to a meridional synthesis of continental and marine core records along the East African Rift–Dead Sea Transform (EARDST) corridor. Owing to its location, the KIND record will yield transformative contributions to climate modeling and to our understanding of climate change in the eastern Mediterranean, a recognized global warming “hotspot”. Moreover, it will document seismic activity along the DST over long timescales, providing a basis for policymakers to prepare for this potential major hazard to infrastructure and human life. Taken together, the KIND project will provide unique and much-needed records from a tectonically active region that is projected to become increasingly arid over the coming century and that is already burdened by severe geopolitical strife. These records are critical for identifying and quantifying regional climate change patterns, assessing seismic risks, and evaluating the ecological impacts of these processes.

item.title: Empirical evidence of overestimated Ku-band sea ice radar freeboards in satellite altimetry
item.dc:creator: Catherine Taelman, Jack C. Landy, Robbie D. C. Mallett, Polona Itkin
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: Arctic, sea ice, satellite altimetry
Arctic sea ice thickness is commonly estimated using radar measurements from satellites. This technique assumes that the snow on sea ice is "invisible" to the radar signals. We studied if this assumption is valid and found that the radar measurements work well in cold conditions, when air temperatures are below –10 °C. However, the radar measurements can overestimate ice thickness during warmer periods, especially if there is new snowfall and if the snow contains salt.

item.title: Deploying machine learning components coupled to Earth System Models with OASIS3-MCT (v6) and Eophis (v1.1)
item.dc:creator: Alexis Barge, Julien Le Sommer, Andrea Storto, Sophie Valcke
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: Earth system model, Earth system, machine learning
Scientists use programs, called Earth System Models, to study and predict climate. These models are based on physical theories but can be completed with AI tools. However, combining these tools with traditional models is difficult due to their different nature. Our research introduces a new method that connects these AI tools with existing climate models. We tested this method by integrating it with an ocean model. This work should help scientists explore new ways of making climate predictions.

item.title: Assessment of snow depth retrievability from passive microwave observations over Arctic sea ice: a global sensitivity analysis
item.dc:creator: Ziyu Yan, Yufang Ye, Georg Heygster, Bin Cheng, Carolina Gabarró, Ferran Hernández-Macià, … (+1)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: Arctic, sea ice, sensitivity analysis
Passive microwave retrieval of snow depth remains constrained by snow and ice conditions. By combining the Snow Microwave Radiative Transfer model with global sensitivity analysis, this study quantifies how snow grain radius, density, and sea ice type affect snow depth retrievability across channels. The small grain radius of new snow limits retrieval performance and increases its sensitivity to sea ice type, while the use of the 89 GHz channel may help address this limitation.

item.title: Hydroclimate Variability at Lake Tana, Ethiopia, Over the Past 6,000 Years: A Critical Synthesis of Geochemical and Isotopic Records
item.dc:creator: Belay Sitotaw Goshu
item.description:
Science Discovery Environment — matched: Holocene, proxy, global warming
Lake Tana, the source of the Blue Nile in the northwestern Ethiopian highlands, is a climatically sensitive archive at the northern margin of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ). Its sediments record changes in the balance between Atlantic/Congo Basin moisture and Indian Ocean/Red Sea moisture, making it a key site for understanding Afro-Asian monsoon dynamics. This review critically synthesizes geochemical (XRF element ratios: Zr/Rb, Ca/Ti, Rb/K) and isotopic (leaf-wax δD) records from Lake Tana to reconstruct hydroclimate variability over the past 6,000 years, evaluate proxy reliability, and identify research gaps. Available evidence indicates that the African Humid Period (AHP) terminated at Lake Tana by approximately 8,000 cal BP, significantly earlier than in the Sahara and North Africa (~5,000 cal BP), δDwax records indicate that this transition was driven by eastward migration of the Congo Air Boundary (CAB), not solely by ITCZ southward retreat. Late Holocene aridification culminated in a pronounced low-stand at ~4,200 cal BP, coeval with the Egyptian Old Kingdom collapse. Existing XRF data (366–150,190 yr) provide a foundation but lack the sampling density needed to resolve centennial-scale variability in the past 6,000 years, and no dedicated high-resolution study exists for the past 2,000 years, a period encompassing the Aksumite civilization and the Little Ice Age. A dedicated high-resolution geochemical and isotopic study is urgently needed to address outstanding questions about natural variability versus anthropogenic impact, and to provide a longer historical context for water resource management in the Blue Nile basin under future global warming.
